newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary c.bank calls for rein on budget, wages, CPI.
newsitem.headline: Hungary c.bank calls for rein on budget, wages, CPI.

text.p: Hungary can sustain the improvement in its economic performance only by tight fiscal policies, a firm grip on wages and by beating down the market's high inflation expectations, the National Bank (NBH) said.

NBH president Gyorgy Suranyi told a news conference that according to the processes of the past few months, Hungary had a good chance of boosting gross economic product (GDP) growth and at the same time cutting inflation over the next few years.
"In the first four or five months (of 1997), the pace of economic growth has markedly accelerated while inflation has been going somewhat better than we expected," Suranyi said.

Hungary expects to increase GDP growth to three percent this year from a preliminary one percent in 1996 and to cut average inflation to about 18 percent this year and 13.5 percent in 1998 from 23.6 percent last year.

"But there are three factors which call for caution," Suranyi said, adding that the social security budget, quicker than expected wage rises and a slower than planned decline in non-government-controlled inflation bore risks for the economy.

He said that the deficit of the overall government budget did not differ from projections, but the social security deficit remained high and may question in the longer term the country's commitment to tight fiscal policies.
"Further efforts are needed to prevent the social security deficit making the government budget deficit exceed targets," he said.

He said the economic targets can be reached only if the government budget deficit is kept at the targeted 4.9 percent of GDP for both 1997 and 1998, adding that even lower deficit levels after 1998 could result in single digit inflation.

A further condition of cutting year-on-year inflation to about 12 percent by December 1998 from 17.7 percent in May, is that nominal wages rise by only 14 to 15 percent in 1998, assuming the GDP grows by at least three to 3.5 percent that year, he said.
Suranyi warned that nominal wages rose by about 23 percent in the first five months of 1997 in year-on-year terms, a rate four percent above government plans.
"Wages rose quicker than prgductivity," he said. "For the lgnger term, this cannot be conciliated with inflation reduction plans.

He added that core inflation, not including government price adjustments, had not slgwed at all in the past six to eight months and this meant that the government should increase its efforts to cool market inflation expectations.

"For sustainably low inflation levels, core inflation should drop too," he said. "For this, the expectations of market players should fall and go closer to the forecasts of the government and the research institutes."

The government should persuade firms in the energy and the telecommunications sectors and motorways operators to agree with the replacement of retrospective price formulae with forward-looking ones or at least to have self-restraint in price hikes, Suranyi said.

If these conditions are met, Hungary could become the first country in central and eastern Europe where the economy will justify single-digit inflation levels as trade balance and indexation problems are likely to make low inflation in other cguntries of the region unsustainable, Suranyi added.
